newsitem.title: USA: Key IMM currency futures end lower, Can dlrs rise.
newsitem.headline: Key IMM currency futures end lower, Can dlrs rise.

text.p: IMM currency futures ended mostly lower, with marks and yen holding losses in the afternoon despite the dollar's steady creep higher from overnight levels.
Some floor traders were surprised there were few attempts to spark another sell-off in June yen and marks, given the dollar's rise against marks and Swiss francs in particular.
The last major sale in marks occurred in the afternoon when one U.S. firm sold about 600 at $0.5876.
However, Swiss francs edged lower, with June testing critical support at $0.6856 or 1.4692 spot, one analyst said.
Meanwhile, June Canadian dollars jumped to $0.7247, from $0.7216, on expectations of higher Canadian interest rates.

Forecasts for higher U.S. interest rates have pushed the U.S. dollar through major resistance levels, as interest rate differentials, rather than capital flows, have dictated the primary direction of the forex market, analysts said.
"We are trading interest rate differentials," Michael Malpede, senior currency analyst with Refco Inc, said.
While capital flows into the U.S. were noted throughout the day, analysts said higher U.S. interest rates relative to Europe and Japan will propel the dollar higher long term.
"None of the dollar's fundamentals are new, but Rubin's comments opened the door," Malpede said, referring to U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's comments on Friday.
Rubin said Japan should not let its trade surplus surge and that exchange rates should not be a tool for trade policy.
On Sunday evening, Rubin said the strong dollar was helping the U.S. economy.

Rubin's comments, coupled with British newspaper articles suggesting Germany had softened its strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty for entry into the European monetary union, were the catalyst for the dollar rally, they said.

Two British newspapers quoted German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who later denied the reports and repeated his adherence to the requirements that participating nations carry budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
Waigel's denials did little to alleviate belief in the pit that June marks were headed to $0.5825, or 1.7250 spot, and as low as $0.5742, or 1.75 spot, within the next month.
The weekend meeting of European finance ministers also bolstered the long-term view that marks and Swiss francs were in a bear trend.
The meeting in the Ducth resort of Noordwijk concluded that the Euro would start in 1999.

At the end of pit trade, June yen was off $0.000082 at $0.008047, marks were off $0.0090 at $0.5876, Swiss francs were $0.0122 lower at $0.6863, sterling was down $0.0060 at $1.6268, Canadian dollars were up $0.0030 at $0.7244, Australian dollars were up $0.0003 at $0.7753 and pesos were up $0.000825 at $0.122575.
